title: Colonial Wounds: Ainu, Australia, and the Stolen Generations
intro: Japan's mirror of Canada, then the film that makes policy personal. Begin Assignment 4.2 here.

terms.def: Judging other peoples by your own culture's standards, the attitude underneath colonial policy everywhere.
Imposed control over land and life, producing the effects the chapter catalogues across continents.

body: Europeans were not the only colonists, and the Ainu of Hokkaido prove the injuries repeat. Fishing, hunting, and gathering peoples met Wajin migrants moving north a thousand years ago, fought six centuries of conflict, then watched their 1669 rebellion die with their poisoned leader Shakushine at supposed peace talks, followed by forced submission and a land-lease system handing settlers fishing, hunting, and timber rights with free rein to exploit. Debt and labour camps came next, with smallpox, cholera, and syphilis; an 1873 decree calling Hokkaido unowned state property invited a million homesteaders; and the 1899 Hokkaido Kyu-Dojin, former Aboriginals, Protection Act confined a non-farming people to unworkable farm scraps, arrested river fishers and woodcutters, and seized land uncultivated within fifteen years until many starved. Only in 1997 did Japan fund Ainu cultural revival for today's roughly 24,000 survivors.

The chapter then hands you the comparison as coursework: research one colonized people outside North America, Australia's Aboriginal peoples, southern Africa's San, or Scandinavia and Russia's Sámi, and build a museum display answering what the colonizer's actions revealed about its worldview, how that worldview compared with the indigenous one, how the experience shapes culture today, and what general statements hold, with Canadian parallels for each. Three presentation modes minimum, pamphlet, slides, artifacts, because the medium is part of the argument.

Australia carries the lesson's heaviest file. Between the 1870s and 1969 about 100,000 indigenous children were taken from their families into institutions or non-indigenous adoptions, a policy meant to erase a distinct people, and Section 127 of the Australian Constitution refused even to count aboriginal natives until its 1967 repeal. Rabbit Proof Fence dramatizes that machinery through children walking home along the fence, and Charles Perkins, taken at ten to an Adelaide mission school where his grandmother could only press her face to the wire, then spotted by English soccer clubs at sixteen, shows the system's other face: systematic racism at home, discovered inferiority abroad, and a return in 1959 to fight instead.

Assignment 4.2 starts now and wants your opinion on the Stolen Generations, why some Australians deny the idea, and what the film's children prove. Watch with the museum-display questions open: colonizer worldview, indigenous worldview, effects today, and the Canadian parallel for each. Perkins's later Freedom Rides and embassy tent belong to Lesson 6's education story; for now, bank the taking itself.

example.title: Assignment 4.2 method
example.text: For each film claim, demand two supports: one scene and one theme source (this chapter, the Stolen Generations fact sheet, or the TRC Calls to Action). Scene plus source is the whole method.

check.prompt: What does the Ainu example prove about colonization?
check.sample: Sample response: that its injuries repeat across continents and colonizers, with the same sequence of land theft, forced labour, banned culture, and starvation reaching the same international forums.

title: What the World Wants from Indigenous Land
intro: Rio's promise, four industries, and the management the world ignored.

terms.def: Meeting today's needs without stealing tomorrow's, the Rio promise that indigenous knowledge must help define.
The 1992 environment-and-development accord stating that resource rights do not override indigenous peoples' rights.

body: Nearly everything manufactured begins in a mine, well, forest, or dam, and the search for more pushes into the most inaccessible places left, which are usually indigenous homelands. Developing countries welcome the income and debt relief, typically arranged with foreign companies and international financing, while indigenous peoples pay in displacement from ancestral lands. The 1992 Rio Declaration on Environment and Development drew the line the rest of this lesson tests: countries may exploit their resources, but that right does not override indigenous peoples' rights, because human beings sit at the centre of sustainable development, entitled to healthy, productive lives in harmony with nature.

Four industries show the line crossed and honoured. Tourism can sustain, as when the Calgary Zoo's partnership with Ghana's Wechiau communities funds a hippopotamus sanctuary that employs locals and saves a species, or invade, as in the Philippines' Cordillera where hotels rose on ancestral land and traditions became merchandise. Mining feeds the industrial world and scars it along every road, river, and power line: Spirit Mountain, sacred to Montana's Assiniboine and A'aninin nations, yielded pollution so badly cleaned that a 1994 lawsuit won local communities $37 million. Hydroelectricity, 19 percent of the world's power and 90 percent in some countries, drowns valleys behind costly dams; southern Alberta's Oldman Dam, built for farmers' water on Piikani traditional land, destroyed First Nations cultural artifacts. And uranium's ledger is written in bodies: Sahtú Dene ore carriers worked brief Arctic summers at the Eldorado mine and later sickened and died of radiation exposure the government never warned them about.

Against extraction stands management the world is only now crediting. Indigenous peoples ran inherently sustainable economies in deserts and the Arctic for millennia, and the 1992 Earth Summit's Rio Declaration finally recognized their vital role in environmental management, urging states to support their identity, culture, and interests and seat them effectively in sustainable development. The chapter's reflection sends you home for proof: find one oral-tradition story from a local Aboriginal group teaching a sustainable practice.

The investigation assignment makes the conflict concrete: take one of five cases, Costa Rica's Boruca dam, Argentina's El Desquite mine, Malaysia's Upper Baram timber, Botswana's Central Kalahari reserve, or Ecuador's Texaco operations, research nature, cause, resolution, and prevention, then report with map, timeline, perspectives, impact analysis, one Canadian connection, and your own recommendation for a better process. The Wichi bulldozer in an Argentine village cemetery, one careless clear-cut among many, is the cover image of the old approach; your report's symbol should propose the new one.

example.title: Test Rio's line
example.text: Run each industry against the Rio sentence: did the right to exploit override indigenous rights here? Tourism in Ghana passes, the Cordillera fails, Spirit Mountain fails, Oldman Dam fails, Eldorado fails catastrophically. Five verdicts, one standard.

check.prompt: What does the Eldorado mine prove about the gap between Rio's promise and practice?
check.sample: Sample response: Sahtú Dene carriers were exposed to lethal radiation without warning or protection, showing resource rights overriding indigenous lives decades before Rio, and the promise still needs enforcement to mean anything.
